item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Alleged spy plot targeting CEO raises questions about Nvidia's future

Alleged spy plot targeting CEO raises questions about Nvidia's future Jensen Huang has been synonymous with Nvidia since he co-founded it more than 30 years ago

The company now faces potential damage to its reputation and stock price, uncertainty over a possible successor and new scrutiny from shareholders and elected officials (Photo: Reuters)

AP San Francisco 5 min read Last Updated : Nov 11 2026 | 7:53 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Investigations into whether Nvidia's CEO was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort" are raising questions about the future of the chipmaker, which became one of the world's most valuable companies by providing technology that powered the artificial intelligence boom. Jensen Huang has been synonymous with Nvidia since he co-founded it more than 30 years ago. The company now faces potential damage to its reputation and stock price, uncertainty over a possible successor and new scrutiny from shareholders and elected officials. President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI is investigating Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. But Trump said he spoke with the executive and believes Huang "had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy."   With a valuation of more than USD 4 trillion, the company has outsized importance as a Wall Street behemoth and provider of chips relied upon by AI developers. Law enforcement and members of Congress, as well as Nvidia's board and shareholders, are all asking questions about the affair. The company's shares dropped more than 4 per cent Monday and continued sinking Tuesday morning.

Nvidia's identity has been tied to Huang himself Huang has said he has more than 60 direct reports in a corporate structure that keeps him at the centre of decision-making. As various investigations ramp up, the succession plan to replace Huang is unclear. "The Nvidia board is between a rock and a hard spot. They have almost no good options. Jensen is Nvidia," said David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School. "And if he has done something wrong and he needs to be removed and they have no successors, that's a terrible outcome."   Replacing Huang would be challenging in part because his public profile is so closely associated with Nvidia.

Also Read

Nvidia CEO's alleged China spy link promised investors access to AI chips

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a professor of leadership at the Yale School of Management, compared Huang's relationship with Nvidia to Steve Jobs' role at Apple. Down to Huang's signature leather jacket, like Jobs' turtleneck, Nvidia is "symbolically and substantively, inextricably intertwined around his personal aura."   Other tech executives, such as Oracle's Larry Ellison and Microsoft's Bill Gates, have also been deeply intertwined with the success of their companies, making it hard to separate them. But in those cases, the companies "can still be successful long after the original founders have taken on a lesser role," said Dan Morgan, vice president and senior portfolio manager at investment firm Synovus Trust.

If Huang resigns or is removed by the board, speculation on possible replacements has turned to figures including Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky, who is a senior technology executive at the company, and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress. Nvidia employs more than 40,000 people worldwide, and there are "lots of other great leaders" within the company, said Bob O'Donnell, president, founder and chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research. "I think it's important that the company starts to let some of these other folks come out as spokespeople so people feel trust, they feel good about Nvidia and their future, even without Jensen," O'Donnell said, although he said he does not think Huang will leave his post.

Huang had the Midas touch, but his reputation is at risk During his 33-year tenure at the helm of Nvidia, Huang built a reputation as a trusted business leader and an established voice within the technology world. He cultivated close relationships with other tech executives, as well as with Trump, helping to persuade him to take a lighter touch on regulating AI. "Everybody wanted to have that Midas touch of his when it comes to technology," O'Donnell said. But the scandal is a growing liability for Huang and Nvidia at a delicate time for the AI industry after the midterm elections in the US ushered in a wave of Democrats promising tougher regulation. Top Democrats Senator Mark Warner and Representative Hakeem Jeffries said Monday they are interested in investigating further.

A shareholder on Monday sued Nvidia and Huang, accusing them of deceiving investors in their responses to media reports about Huang's affair with the purported Chinese spy. The complaint filed in a California court says the company misled investors about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, who news reports said is suspected of working for Chinese intelligence, and the national security implications. The New York Times identified her as a business executive and Chinese citizen. Sonnenfeld said he places the odds that Huang stays on as CEO at roughly 50-50, but those odds are "slipping by the moment."   "He has lost the confidence and trust of his key constituents, his board, his employees," said Sonnenfeld, who is also founder and president of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute. "And every employee knows that if anybody else had done this, they would have been fired long ago."   Some experts are more confident in the company's stability going forward. Morgan, of Synovus Trust, said that if Huang is required to step down to a lesser role at Nvidia following the company's investigation, he is "still confident that the company will continue to maintain its lead in the GPU AI chip market."   But at the same time, the affair "sounds more like a made-for-TV melodrama than a real story," he said.

item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Dreams, desks and selfies: New US lawmakers learn their way around

Dreams, desks and selfies: New US lawmakers learn their way around More than 100 newly elected lawmakers have arrived in Washington for orientation ahead of taking office on January 3

The US Capitol in Washington | Image: Bloomberg

AP Washington 6 min read Last Updated : Nov 11 2026 | 7:52 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Representative-elect LaKesha Womack, a community organiser who stunned her own Democratic Party by defeating a well-know North Carolina Republican on her shoestring $56,000 campaign budget, said she's excited to arrive in Washington and show what's possible. Representative-elect Brian Poindexter said his win over incumbent GOP Representative Max Miller ensures Ohio remains a very swing state. And Rebecca Bennett, a former Navy helicopter pilot in New Jersey who said she's spent her whole life "trying to find the biggest, hardest problem to throw myself at," was ready to give Congress a try. "There's always the unknown."   They were among more than 100 newly elected members of Congress arriving in Washington this week for the start of freshmen orientation -- the crush of new Democrats, many bringing a new sense of urgency after the party's sweep of the midterm elections, and the slim new class of freshmen Republicans.

"People were just looking for somebody who's going to listen to them," said Womack, who said she won by simply showing up and talking with voters. "I'm a single mom and so I know what it's like to have to live on a budget and figure out how am I going to feed my family," she said. "And that's what people want to fight for them in Washington right now."   New-member orientation creates an unusual mash-up on Capitol Hill, as the newcomers are arriving and the exiting lawmakers begin to clear out, all in preparation for the peaceful transfer of power on January 3, when lawmakers are sworn in and the new Congress begins.

Also Read

This week's orientation includes training sessions and ritzy receptions for the newcomers, and for the defeated or retirees it's the start of figuring out what's next. Briefing rooms are filled with information about office set up, payroll and benefits, and there's a room to take officials portraits. It's also the time for the House and Senate to hold internal party elections for their new leaders, ahead of a public vote in January for the speaker of the House. "I'm looking forward to learning as much as I can and being the best representative I can be for my district," said Poindexter as he arrived at the nearby Navy Yard hotel where lawmakers are temporarily housed.

Selfies, besties and tough votes ahead The Capitol was a changed place as the members-elect started meeting up with their colleagues and getting to know their way around the place. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan was swarmed by young people in the Capitol basement, taking pictures with the progressive star who is also the first Muslim in the Senate. Texas Senator-elect James Talarico paid a visit to the outgoing Texas Republican Senator John Cornyn, who lost his own primary for reelection when President Donald Trump backed his rival, Ken Paxton, who was defeated. "I'm so grateful for his advice and his guidance as I try to fill his big shoes," Talarico said of Cornyn as he walked through the Senate between orientation events. He said he wants to meet with Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas as well.

And Senator-elect Juliana Stratton of Illinois snapped a photo with new Democratic senators-elect including Talarico, El-Sayed, Annie Andrews, Roy Cooper, Peggy Flanagan, Josh Turek and others. "First Freshmen Senator selfie! Couldn't ask for a better team," she posted as the caption. Among them was former Ohio Senator Sherrod Brown, who defeated Republican Senator Jon Husted, a Trump-backed favourite, for a comeback. Brown was in the Senate for 18 years before he lost two years ago to GOP Senator Bernie Moreno, but he still joined his freshmen colleagues for their orientation. "I've actually learned some things," said Brown, who was celebrating his 74th birthday on Monday. "I've gotten to know my colleagues."

Leadership elections test the new members One of the first decisions the incoming lawmakers will make happens even before they're sworn into office, as they huddle with their parties in private meetings to choose House and Senate leadership. Congressional offices are being bombarded with phone calls and social media messages pushing Democrats to dump their current choices -- House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer -- in favour of a fresh start. Jeffries scoffed when questioned Monday if he had support-- the typically low-key leader flashing confidence he would have the votes. He is on track to make history as the nation's first Black American to become speaker of the House.

Progressive lawmakers, in particular, are agitating for change reflective of voters' sweeping turnout for Democrats, especially in the Senate. Senator-elect Chris Pappas, Democrat-New Hampshire -- who was darting back and forth between his day job as an outgoing member of the House and his new one as an incoming senator -- said their class is "a new generation of leadership that wants to do things differently and shake up Washington."   He said he wants to meet with Schumer and will later decide who he will support, if anyone challenges him. Republicans will also choose their new leaders after House Speaker Mike Johnson decided to step aside following the party's election defeat. Tuesday's closed-door race between the No. 2 Republican Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Ohio Representative Jim Jordan is a repeat of the contest in 2023, before Johnson rose to power.

Representative Richard Hudson, the House GOP campaign chairman who lost his own reelection bid in North Carolina, hesitated to assess the outcome. Besides, he said, he doesn't have a vote in the matter -- the exiting lawmakers are blocked from the GOP meeting. A diverse new class arrives As the week began, the House Chaplain Margaret Kibben opened Monday's session with a prayer, "some of us enjoying victories and others enduring disheartening defeats."   On the Democratic side, the new Congress will see many milestones -- Flanagan will be the first Native American female US senator, Pappas the first gay male senator, and more. Representative Suzan DelBene, the House Democrats campaign chief, called the party's candidates "all very unique."   "We had firefighters, ministers, mayors, veterans, teachers, farmers, prosecutors, union leaders, law enforcement, doctors, journalists and even a Grammy-award winning musician," she said earlier.

"They understand that their job title is representative, not rubber stamp."   Johnson, the outgoing speaker, hosted a reception in the Capitol's stately Statuary Hall for the House Republicans, whose shrinking numbers left the party lopsided, their minority made up of mostly white men.

Eisenkot targets Netanyahu-era policies as new Israeli parliament convenes Eisenkot, a former military chief, has up to six weeks to form a government that would end the tenure of Israel's longest-serving prime minister

Gadi Eisenkot | Image: Reuters

AP Tel Aviv 4 min read Last Updated : Nov 11 2026 | 7:51 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Gadi Eisenkot, the politician tasked with forming a new Israeli government, pledged on Tuesday to reverse many of Benjamin Netanyahu's policies as the new parliament was sworn in. The pledge sets the stage for a consequential month of legislative action and coalition negotiations. Eisenkot, a former military chief, has up to six weeks to form a government that would end the tenure of Israel's longest-serving prime minister. While it remains unclear whether Eisenkot will be able to forge a coalition government, the new Knesset can enact legislation in the meantime. Netanyahu's opponents now control a solid majority in parliament. Eisenkot's bloc introduced a series of bills at the start of the legislative session that target Netanyahu and his policies. They include launching an official government-led inquiry into Hamas' October 7, 2023, attacks, setting term limits on the position of prime minister and overturning changes the outgoing Netanyahu-led government made to limit the powers of the judiciary. It was not immediately clear how quickly or far those bills would advance in the weeks ahead.

Competing calls for unity The former general, who campaigned as a no-nonsense straight shooter, reiterated on Tuesday that his goal was a government that all Israelis could trust, not one that represents only certain factions. Also Read

"We will act for all citizens of Israel, those who voted for us and those who did not, out of deep commitment," Eisenkot said ahead of the Knesset swearing-in ceremony. Netanyahu has sought to undermine the certified election results after his bloc fell short of a majority. He has repeated unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties "stole" the elections. In a speech following Tuesday's ceremony, Netanyahu attacked opposition leaders who have signalled a willingness to partner with Arab parties to form a government. Eisenkot has left that possibility open if the parties meet several conditions, including accepting Israel's identity as a Jewish state and declaring Hamas a terrorist group.

"I ask you: are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?" Netanyahu said. Eisenkot called the speech "divisive" and "hate-filled." Netanyahu's opponents already have a legislative agenda Eisenkot's bloc also triggered a process on Tuesday to install a new parliamentary speaker as they kicked off work on their legislative agenda. A majority of members submitted signatures calling for the ousting of the current Netanyahu-backed speaker, Amir Ohana, the first step toward a vote on his replacement. The vote can take place even before a coalition government is in place. The Knesset speaker is a powerful position. The speaker determines what bills the Knesset will take up, meaning one picked from among the Eisenkot-led opposition parties could propel their legislative agenda forward.

The opposition nominated Matan Kahana, a senior member of Eisenkot's Yashar party, for the job. A vote to appoint him speaker could come as early as this week. Netanyahu as caretaker The swearing-in of the new Knesset ushered in an unusual transitional period in Israeli politics -- Netanyahu and his Cabinet remain in power, while the new lawmakers can introduce legislation. Meanwhile, Eisenkot will meet with party leaders as he works to build a coalition that would likely make him prime minister. If he fails, Israeli President Isaac Herzog is expected to give Netanyahu the next opportunity to form a government. As caretaker prime minister, Netanyahu faces court-imposed limits on his powers. But he can still pursue appointments and could try to block new legislation. He retains full authority over national security, including the military.

Netanyahu has argued that Jewish-led parties should form a unity government to counter the threat of an Iranian attack. He renewed that call Tuesday, urging them to "set aside all other considerations," and said Israel should work to topple the Iranian government. A governing coalition without Netanyahu could leave him politically vulnerable as he faces an ongoing corruption trial and possible findings of security failures in the lead-up to the October 7 attacks.

item.title: US set to become first country to fully shun UN Human Rights Council review
item.description: The United States is set to become the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the UN's top rights body since it was created two decades ago.
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / US set to become first country to fully shun UN Human Rights Council review

US set to become first country to fully shun UN Human Rights Council review Trump administration declines to participate in the UN Human Rights Council's Universal Periodic Review, which examines the rights records of all 193 member states every four to five years

The United States, under Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago | Image: Bloomberg

AP Geneva 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 10 2026 | 2:47 PM IST

Listen to This Article

The United States is set to become the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the UN's top rights body since it was created two decades ago. The Trump administration last year pulled the US out of the Human Rights Council, accusing it of an anti-US and anti-Israel bias, and alleging that it didn't uphold the very values it promotes. Supporters back the council's mandate to keep tabs on human rights in all UN member states including the US, which has drawn criticism for its policies including strong-arm deportations and targeted killings of alleged drug-runners in the Caribbean and Pacific - which the administration has said are designed to protect US workers and help keep the country safe.

The Geneva-based council regularly examines the rights records of all 193 UN member states - generally about every four to five years - as part of a process known as the universal periodic review. The United States, under Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago. The scheduled November 2025 review was pushed back until Tuesday in hopes that the US government might change its mind. Also Read

It did not. "(W)e give no credibility to the agency," a State Department spokesperson said in an email to The Associated Press. "This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own values' as it pushes anti-American rhetoric," the spokesperson said, alleging the council's "persistent failure to condemn the most egregious human rights violators."   The council says the process requires participation of the country in question, and in the case of an absence of any national representatives, the review cannot go forward.

As part of such reviews, national delegations - which at times can include a dozen officials or more - make a presentation, face questions and hear recommendations from other national envoys. It's supposed to be a sweeping and constructive process, akin to holding up a mirror to governments to improve their human rights policies. Critics of the US snub warn that the walkout could encourage other countries - many of which bristle about intense scrutiny from human rights monitors - to follow suit. Jamil Dakwar, director of the American Civil Liberties Union's human rights program, said: "The administration is saying to the world, we don't care about whether you would review us or not, we're going to continue to violate human rights unabashed'."   "And we are saying: No, enough is enough. This council should hold the United States accountable'," he told reporters Monday in Geneva, as part of a push by civil society to raise awareness about the US rights record.

He said the ACLU and allies have called on the UN human rights chief to respond by presenting an update on rights in the United States early next year. Eric Tistounet, a visiting professor at the Geneva Graduate Institute who was the council's first secretary, said the US walkout could affect the credibility of the council's review system. "If the predominant global power - which has always claimed to adhere to the human rights norms - doesn't show up and doesn't even justify why, then you are in big trouble," he said.
